BV Bicycle Strap-On Saddle Bag with perfect Size I With reflective for a Safety ride I Seat Bag, Cycling Bag - Bike Bag for all our essentials, bike bags for bicycles, bicycle bag, bike seat bag Can't remember why I bought this instead of a known cycling brand (Topeak, Lezyne, Ortleib, etc). Must have been desperate to get something fast without going to the store? Anyway, this bag has failed after 4 years. I've never before seen a bag in this category fail. Generally they just last until a new style sucpercedes the old one. E.g. when I was a kid everyone used those barrel-shaped bags that attached through those little belt loop tabs on the backs of touring saddles. I saw those in my parents' garage decades later, dirty but still intact.

I have had straps get fuzzy but never wear through. I have broken a strap on a bikepacking bag under heavy load on rough roads.

Never had stitching fail with no obvious cause. It just wasn't put together as well as the brand name stuff, I guess. Anyway, I would recommend sticking with the known brands for this type item. IMHO a saddle bag needs to just sit quietly until it's needed, and I don't want to ever worry about it doing its job. I wouldn't trust this bag again.

text_fidelity_a:
MBB Ab Equipment,Home Ab Machine Function Movement Multiple Core Strength, Abdominal Training 10 in 1 Magic Body Builder with 3 Levels Resistance for Teenage,Women and Men.122 Country Patented I was excited to try this as I love fitness gadgets, and when they added a $10 off coupon, I ordered it even though I read reviews on another brand of the same item from shorter people that it was too big. Turns out for me, they were right. I'm 5' 3", and this is uncomfortable to use to do ab crunches with as it's so long it presses into the top front of my shoulders instead of my upper chest or below, which gets pretty painful after a few reps.

The manufacturer's claim their low resistance level is about 35 pounds of resistance (16kg in pounds) is not true of my unit. I measured the resistance. Moving the smaller side toward the larger only a few inches using a calibrated spring scale, the resistance was 55 pounds - I couldn't move it further as my wrists aren't that strong, but I'd guess it gets to around 75 pounds of resistance when fully compressed.

For upper body moves, over 55 pounds is way too much for someone who isn't already pretty fit. People who have been sedentary, have had injuries or who just aren't that strong could hurt themselves trying to close it or just become frustrated as they wouldn't be able move the two sides together. If you're getting this hoping to start to get fit, it's going to be too strong. At over 55 pounds of resistance if you're under I'd think 5' 8" or taller, the abdominal exercise in the third image is going to hurt - in the picture, the woman has this under her armpit, but think about pushing 60 pounds of pressure with your armpit - ouch! I tried pushing against it with my chest rather than my armpit, but it was too tall. And the padding, which would probably be adequate for resistance of up to 30 pounds, isn't thick enough at over 50 - it presses deeply and slightly painfully into my thighs for adductions.

I do use this for hip adductions - where you put it between your thighs and squeeze. It's pretty challenging, and I am used to doing 100 to 130 pound adductions at the gym, but the ergonomics of the MBB Ab Equipment make most movements more difficult. It shoots out from under me when I try to do some of the floor exercises pictured like what they call "SIDE WAIST" and "WAIST TRAINING"; for the one they call waist training, the Wondercore Smart is better as you can adjust the resistance, it starts out less open, and it's more stable on the floor.

This could be useful to add to your at-home workouts. If you're already pretty strong - not a bodybuilder, but have worked out your chest and arms regularly at over 40 pounds, this unit could be useful. If you haven't, it's going to be very difficult, and I'd recommend you use one of the many thigh master units available here on Amazon, a spring power twister or something like this https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00OZ0HECI/ with padding on the arms - I use barbell shoulder pads on the arms of mine. It was good for me for hips and inner thighs, but I've been working them regularly for a while now. I wasn't able to use this for everything they claim, but the MBB Ab Equipment is great for hip adductions, okay for chest if I'm careful.
text_fidelity_b: MBB Ab Equipment,Home Ab Machine Function Movement Multiple Core Strength, Abdominal Training 10 in 1 Magic Body Builder with 3 Levels Resistance for Teenage,Women and Men.122 Country Patented

It opens easily, has a good balance and feel in the hand, and locks securely. Whether stabbing or cutting, it does a good job. I had to work a bit to cut some poly rope, but it wasn't completely unreasonable.

However, there's a big negative (for me). I find the lock poorly designed and therefore really awkward to use when closing the knife. You have to push a metal flange that's inside the handle, and hold it while you're closing the blade towards your fingers. Sure, you can pause the motion, move your fingers out of the way, and then close the knife safely. But I've seen much better locking mechanisms that didn't require this kind of maneuver. text_fidelity_a: BBAhandware 27.7x18.2x16 in Folding Table Portable Large Camping Table Ultra Light Folding Beach Table Camping with Carrying Bag,Withstands Weights of Up to 55lbs (Silver) I'm not a serious prepper or anything, but I did live 5 days last February without power during the blizzard in Texas.  I have spent the subsequent months getting ready for another time like that again.  The video I watched was a cool way to heat an area in your house when the power is off.  I already had the rectangular paving stones/bricks to place on this table as well as the little alcohol burners.  The idea is to place the cement stones/bricks (the flat ones, not the large ones with holes in them) around the alcohol burner.  The alcohol burner transfers heat to the bricks which in turn release the stored heat over a longer time in the area where they are set up.  Obviously this can't be set up on the floor, so a table that can handle the stored heat is what I needed.  I set the cement blocks up on this metal camping table, put the alcohol burner in the middle and let it "work."  This camping table is the perfect size for my emergency room warming set up with the bricks an burner.  I know it will work fine for a table to use my propane cookstove on as well, but for the moment it is in an emergency box in my house along with the cement bricks and the alcohol burner (and a bottle of rubbing alcohol).  I'm very happy with how this table worked out for my purposes.
text_fidelity_b: BBAhandware 27.7x18.2x16 in Folding Table Portable Large Camping Table Ultra Light Folding Beach Table Camping with Carrying Bag,Withstands Weights of Up to 55lbs (Silver)

text_fidelity_a:
EXERPEUTIC EXERWORK 2000i Bluetooth Folding Exercise Desk Bike with 24 Workout Programs and Free App Ordered in October and it is now February. 4 months of use. Sort of.
The exercise-work-bike took a total of 3 days to put together, and had I been doing it alone, I probably never would have gotten it. There is some form of blue “insta-glue” on the pedal screws that made them nearly impossible to screw in. 3 neighborhood kids and teenagers tried their best to help a lady out, but to no avail. Eventually, I hung my head in shame and begged the assistance of male-friend to demonstrate his masculinity and wield tools to get the pedal screwed in.
I am 5’8. That’s 68 inches or about 172cm.
The next issue came when I realized that even at the lowest adjustment, the one recommended for 5’1-5’4 heights, I still struggled to reach the pedals, sitting with my back comfortably against the backrest. If I scooched forward just enough that half my cheeks were off the front of the seat I could reach the pedals, the backrest, and still use the desk for my laptop! But the desk was still a bit high, so I used the tilt-a-table adjustment to relax my wrists and type with perfectly non-ergonomical T-Rex arms.
And now the clunking noise. I can’t stand it. It started off quiet, but after maybe 100 miles of use, it makes a clunking noise from the pedals and no matter how many times I tighten the bolts (almost to stripping them), the seat keeps wobbling and the handle bars offer very little support.

Overall, as a workout bike, it give options that a regular bike doesn’t have—a table.
As for the rest, I am very unhappy with the very little use I got out of it, the lack of structural support for a solid working/workout of cycling, and how fast it has started having issues.
text_fidelity_b: EXERPEUTIC EXERWORK 2000i Bluetooth Folding Exercise Desk Bike with 24 Workout Programs and Free App

text_fidelity_a:
94 Piece First Aid Kit Packed with First Aid and Survival Essential by Sirius Survival A good first aid kit is a good thing to keep in the car when traveling and I selected this kit to keep in one of the vehicles because all of us are road warriors these days. Of course, the hope is that it is never needed, but when one is needed it's an invaluable resource. This is an interesting kit, and it has some pluses and minuses.

This is a small kit that fits nicely under a seat, in a seat pocket, or in a center console. Finding a place for it in a car or truck should be no issue at all.

There's a lot going on in this kit. It has a lot of the typical first aid items - bandages, gauze, cotton swabs, anticeptic wipes, and even a foil emergency blanket. There's some really odd things in here too - a flint, a compass, a whistle and a multi-tool are the stand-outs. This is not a typical first-aid kit but is also a basic survival kit.

The multi-tool is the standout in the whole kit and is worth the cost of the whole kit. It seems to be made fairly well, it is heavier than some of the cheaper ones I have seen and used and it has the basic tools you'd expect - pliers, a knife, screwdriver, etc. It includes a set of bits as well.

The compass is relatively cheap but it does work.

The remainder of the components in this kit are farily nondescript. All will work in an emergency capacity.

As a first aid kit this isn't so bad. However, this thing tries to be a survival kit as well, and on that basis there's an important omission - there's no flashlight in this kit. Even a small $5 flashlight would make this kit more complete and capable.

This certainly isn't a bad kit, but it tries to be two different things and as a survival kit it comes up a little short. This will serve well for a traveling family and in a pinch it will make a decent emergency kit, but I would not rely on it as a sole source.
text_fidelity_b: 94 Piece First Aid Kit Packed with First Aid and Survival Essential by Sirius Survival

text_fidelity_a:
Thule Compass Kayak and SUP roof Rack - Carries 2 Kayaks or 2 SUPs - J-Style Carrier - Universal mounting Hardware Included - Fits 36" Wide Kayaks and SUPs - 130lb Weight Limit I am surprised to see myself giving a Thule product a less than perfect score. The only reason is that it doesn't come with integrated locks. Here I thought everything they had used their "one key" system (and of course by making you buy locks separately, you can ensure you get the correct cylinders to match your existing key...but let's face it, buying separately gets expensive...and is onerous). So I guess you can buy new straps that have locks built in...I'm guessing they have a steel wire inside as further theft deterrent. And you may be able to buy lock cylinders and/or additional hardware to lock the carrier to the car racks. But anyway, none of this is included, so I cannot be impressed (or not) how seamless it all is. For a product in this price range, I expect the best in every way.

And it is likely the best in every other way. I mean, I can't give it less than a four because it is a great - and somewhat versatile - carrier. I have another generic kayak carrier that I've been using for a while, and now I hate that one - can't believe I ever put up with it. Thule really does seem to sit and think and overthink their seemingly simple items to create the best. And then pick materials to match. The quality of the materials is just magnificent, especially when you think that this is strictly for utility.

While I would still recommend this carrier, I'd do so with the caveat that you see what other options that have as far as included security features and/or what it would take to get this as secure as you want it to be. I realize some people don't care about this feature.
text_fidelity_b: Thule Compass Kayak and SUP roof Rack - Carries 2 Kayaks or 2 SUPs - J-Style Carrier - Universal mounting Hardware Included - Fits 36" Wide Kayaks and SUPs - 130lb Weight Limit

text_fidelity_a:
Dechunxian Best Collapsible Cup Foldable Silicone Sports Water Bottle Camping Canteens 550ml (Blue) This has to be one of the oddest water bottles I've come across. It's made of silicon, which means it's all squishy and soft to the touch. I had my doubts when I first took it out of the package, but it really works well and offers benefits that I don't have with my other bottles.

The main benefit is that you can roll the bottle up into a pretty tight bundle. It comes with a silicon band (about the size of a typical rubber band) to hold the bottle when it's folded. That feature is great for traveling - when you're done with the water, just fold up the bottle and tuck it away. It will easily fit into a pocket when folded.

The soft silicone also has a benefit when the bottle is filled. I usually carry a metal water bottle in my messenger bag, and have received a poke in the ribs on more than one occasion from the bottle shifting around. This silicon is much nicer - no hard edges to poke me in the ribs. It also has a carabineer clip on the top so it can be clipped onto a bag, backpack or belt.

Despite the soft feel, this is pretty durable. I have not had any problems with it tearing or splitting, and I'm not all that gentle on my water bottles. The silicon is thick enough that I'm confident it will stand up to a good amount of use. It has a flip-top cover that is easy to open one-handed. Since it's silicon, you can squeeze the bottle and have the water shoot out rather than have to tilt the bottle back to take a drink. It's a nice feature to have when you're using this while exercising.

The only downside to the silicon is that it's not the best choice for use in a car cup holder. The sides will bend in, making it less than ideal in terms of stability. It does stand on its own when filled, but can be a bit bendy when it's partially filled. This is much more of an on-the-go type of bottle.

It feels rather odd, doesn't look like a bottle at all when you get it folded up, but it works extremely well as an easy way to take water along without having to deal with the size and weight of a metal bottle, or the fixed shape of a plastic bottle. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Dechunxian Best Collapsible Cup Foldable Silicone Sports Water Bottle Camping Canteens 550ml (Blue)

text_fidelity_a:
Weaver Leather Throw Line Storage Bag Are you a ham radio operator tossing portable antennas up into trees? Don't like the idea of sling shots and potato launchers? Hate that tangled mess of mason line? Looking for reasonable elevation for the weekend? I recommend this.

I hate rope, string, wine, wire, cable, and anything squiggly that is over 25 feet long. It is certain to become a tangled mess and cost 30 minutes to an hour to straighten out just to have it wrap around your ankle and trip you up. Happens to me every single time.

Some smart ham out there suggested I try this throw line bag and weight. After it was delivered I brought it out to the backyard and started tossing it around. I made about five or six long low tosses without any tangles and three or four high tosses over the tree without a problem. I'm sold on it. My slingshot is going to see a lot less use and I still don't have the guts to try my potato launcher.

The bag is more than storage. After a toss you just stuff the line back in the bag without concern for winding it properly. Just push it down in the bag. When tossing the weight you just let the line play out of the bag. I have yet to experience a tangle. I'm sure there's some added resistance and I might be losing a foot or two of max height but for ease of storage and deployment you can have the foot.

When done, stuff the line in the bag along with the weight. Cinch it up and toss back in the truck until next time. Not a whole lot of fussing.

A warning... wear gloves. The rope they use burns! Me and one other person found out the hard way. Ya... I didn't tell him. But even after that he went out and bought his own kit so maybe the burn wasn't so bad. Still, wear gloves.

I think I got the 12 oz weight. Then next one down might have been a little better. After a few tosses of the 12 oz weight I was getting real tired and my height/distance was dropping rapidly. Good argument for doing it right the first time I guess. Still, 8 oz might be some benefit.

I know it's tempting but don't toss this thing at your buddies. The weight is substantial and if you hit them they won't share in your amusement. Not that I did anything like that but you know. It could happen.

That's it. Wish I found this a long time ago. Until now I had been using my slingshot with a 1 oz weight and a Zebco 33 and 20 lb test line. Then I would tie the mason line for the second pass. The tangles were unbelievable so a spool of mason line was a one-time-use item for me. The rope in this kit is strong enough to hold up any wire antenna for a weekend so you only need a single pass.
text_fidelity_b: Weaver Leather Throw Line Storage Bag

text_fidelity_a:
Pelican Dayventure Backpack Soft Cooler Going on hikes is a regular way of life for me. If the hike is more than a few miles in length, then I must have a backpack loaded with the essentials, both for survival and for enjoyment. I want a backpack suitable for my lifestyle/desires and a backpack that provides what I need is the Pelican Elite Backpack Cooler.

This backpack is different from others than I own and use. It has two compartments: an upper, 13 liter compartment and a lower, 5.4 liter compartment. The backpack is well insulated overall and is made with material that feels like that of a tent. It is well protected from the elements and you can feel confident that, wherever you go, the contents of your backpack will remain in workable/usable condition.

What sets this backpack apart from most others is the bottom compartment. It is designed to hold canned beverages and it can hold up to eight cans, standing upright. This section is kept sealed by a heavy zipper that takes effort to open and close, but that provides peace of mind. The bottom section keeps beverages cold by way of its insulation, but I recommend adding an ice pack or two for the highest level of protection. As long as your ice pack is thin in design, it should work. And if you have items that need to be kept cold in the top compartment, then adding an ice pack there is also a good idea.

This backpack straps on easily and is generally comfortable to use. It is more rigid than my other backpacks but also better insulated and better able to protect the contents from the elements. It is just right for people like me who tend to carry more food and drink in my backpack than anything else. I would like it If the top section was sealed more thoroughly with a heavy zipper similar to what you get with the bottom compartment. But this is still a useful backpack overall and one I like to use for my frequent day hikes in local parks.
text_fidelity_b: Pelican Dayventure Backpack Soft Cooler

text_fidelity_a:
OKAI EA10 Electric Scooter with Seat, Up to 25-35 Miles Range & 15.5MPH, Moped Scooter Bike for Adults with 10 Inch Vacuum Tires Set up of the scooter is a fairly simple process. The only downside is putting on the bike seat. It doesn’t slide down very easily and isn’t fully secure, the seat swivels back and forth which can be inconvenient.

The scooter in general is great and able to take me from point A to point B in a timely manner. One feature that really makes the scooter user friendly is the battery. Being able to take the battery out and leave the scooter outside while charging it inside is extremely convenient.

The keys that come with the scooter are also extremely convenient. With the NFC feature it’s easy to unlock, all you have to do is touch the key to the scooter’s digital interface.

Making sure you have enough battery is important if you are planning on going somewhere far. The gauge on the scooter doesn’t give you an accurate idea of how far you can go, and the apps percentages aren’t very accurate either.

One other thing I wish it had was a longer pole. It is tall enough for my hand to reach it when I’m standing but it has to be fully extended so it can be awkward and unsafe. If it was a little bit longer, it’d be perfect for sitting and standing.

It is most comfortable to ride while sitting but you are able to stand. Depending on your height, standing may feel comfortable or a bit awkward. If you’re around the 6ft range it feels slightly too short to use while standing, although it is possible. It would've been nice if some adjustments have been made in the scooter so that it would have been easy to use both sitting and standing.

The scooter is really easy to operate. Right out of the box, all you do is turn it on and go. The acceleration is quick and the brakes are fast and efficient.

The scooter is made in China and being sold by Chinese company on Amazon. At the current price of 700 bucks I'm sure it's at least 250 bucks over priced.
text_fidelity_b: OKAI EA10 Electric Scooter with Seat, Up to 25-35 Miles Range & 15.5MPH, Moped Scooter Bike for Adults with 10 Inch Vacuum Tires

text_fidelity_a:
Osprey Discontinued Osprey Salida 8 Women's Bike Hydration Backpack with Hydraulics Reservoir, Teal Glass [[VIDEOID:f899b5904dd638d027a40416fde9e9f1]] This is my first hydration pack and it does not come with any instructions. It took me about one hour to figure everything out--particularly the hydration bladder. However, after using this, I love it. It is extremely well designed, comfortable, and stylish. I also love the color.

PROS
- There's a loop for a light on the bottom of the pack.

- It has a bike helmet clip.

- There's an outer pocket to store clothing.

- The inner pocket has one covered zippered pocket for cell phone, Chapstick, etc. There's also a mesh zippered pocket below that and another folder-like pocket opposite that in addition to the main compartment area for minimal storage.

- Behind the inner pocket is the zippered compartment for the hydration bladder.

- The hydration bladder is 2.5L or 85 ounces. It comes with a handle and the pack has a tiny cinch strap that holds the bladder upright when full so that it does not sink to the bottom of the pack. I did a search on YouTube for "How to fill Osprey Hydration pack," and found Chris SERF's very helpful video. Prior to viewing that video I just could not figure out how to open the main bladder compartment after I got the slide cinch off the bladder.

- The pack has a waist belt and a chest belt with magnetic closure.

- The tubing to the reservoir has a magnetic disk that clips it onto the chest belt area of the pack. There are also various loops through which the tubing can pass.

- The bite valve is removable. Another YouTuber said there is a locking mechanism to lock the bite valve but I could not get it to lock. Sometimes water will leak out of the bite valve but I only had that happen once.

- It has a mesh back to increase air flow which reduces but does not eliminate sweating against the pack.

CONS
- This comes with zero instructions and I could not find a video on the Osprey website on how to fill the hydration bladder. As of this writing, there are also no manuals for the Salida under the customer support section.

- The tubing is about two inches too short for my build. Since the card that came with the pack says the tubing can be cut, I think the tubing should be lengthened as it can always be made shorter but it is impossible to make longer.

- My major complaint is that the water coming out of the bladder tastes awful. It tastes like a new shower curtain smells. I was only able to drink about half a cup as I kept spitting it out. I wrote and tweeted Osprey and they have not yet responded with a solution. However, the YouTuber, Chris MORSF, whose video helped me learn how to open the bladder said that the "Only thing that I can think of is Steriliser tablets like what is used for babies bottles then giving the bladder a very thorough rinse out with water." I have yet to try that.

Overall, I love the way this pack is engineered and how comfortable it is. I used this once so far on a two-hour walk and I did not even know I was wearing this. I had a concern of drying the bladder between use but came up with my own solution of stuffing the bladder mouth with a silicone ramekin (see last photo) and hanging it upside down for several days. It dried in two days and the tubing is almost dry as of day three. If Osprey addressed all three CONS and provided instructions or a link to instructions for a neophyte user like me and how to get rid of that bad taste, I would have rated this five stars. I attached a video that I hope is helpful and some pictures of this Osprey Salida 8 Women's pack.

UPDATE May 14, 2019 - I finally heard from Osprey regarding the two questions I had. I have yet to try either solution.

1 – To get rid of the disgusting plastic flavor of the water, they recommend freezing the reservoir with lemon juice to clean it out. They also have cleaning tablets available that help with the taste.

2- With regard to the bite valve lock being unmovable, they recommend running it under hot water and then twisting it.
text_fidelity_b: Osprey Discontinued Osprey Salida 8 Women's Bike Hydration Backpack with Hydraulics Reservoir, Teal Glass

Confidence Power Plus Motorized Fitness Treadmill White I should have put this unit together within thirty days but I had other projects that took priority. When I finally opened the box, there were two problems: 1) the directions were terrible; and 2) two screw holes at the base were shorn off. (I think someone had sent the unit back because of this problem, and then, it was sent to me because the exterior box was a bit worn. Let’s put it that way.) The good news is I figured out how to put the unit together myself, without directions, and the shorn screw holes were not vital for the operation of the machine or visible unless you look closely.
Assembly:
There are three screws with a plastic cap. Two are big and one is small. The large ones go behind the monitor and at the bottom of the unit in the front. The small one goes on the left side of the unit in the front. There are two plastic covers that go at the foot of the back of the unit on each side. They screw in with four screws. (Again, I could only use two screws because two of the screw holes were stripped.) That is it for assembly. It was relatively easy to assemble, and the unit works well. I am 5’9” and don’t fall off of it. I like that there are no rails on the side to run into. text_fidelity_a:
Withings Pulse Wireless Activity Tracker + Sleep and Heart Rate Monitoring, Black UPDATE 1/17/2015

I had this for a year, and loved using it -- until it stopped working. I had purchased 6 of these in total (5 as gifts), and at least 2/6 of these things no longer hold a charge. When I emailed support, because I contacted them just over the year mark (Jan 6th purchase date), the best they could offer me was a 25% discount. It's great when it works, but such a high failure rate within a year seems disappointing.

==========================
The Withings Pulse claims to track your activity, your sleep, and your heart rate.

If you're looking for something that is precise and accurate for exactly what you've done, this isn't it. I don't think the technology is quite there yet in any device.

But if you're looking for something that is effective as a motivator, and that gives you a consistent baseline to measure your progress, this is perfect for that.

I've been eyeing activity trackers for some time. Many of my friends choose the Fitbit while others chose the Nike Fuel band. I finally pulled the trigger on this device specifically for a few reasons:

1. Integration with a smart scale. I think if you're really motivated to change yourself - get more active, lose some weight, you want to get the smart scale with it to close the loop. It is that much more rewarding and encouraging to keep up with your daily goal if you see the results of your work (whether it's lower fat %, lower weight). The Fitbit also has a scale, but I liked that the Withings scale had been around for longer. Sure you could just get any scale and put in manual measures to your app, but I'm a lazy person and having all of that integrated and automatically synchronized is a big deal.

2. Works for both iPhone and Android. I can't find the studies right now, but it's far easier to get fit and stay healthy if everyone else is doing it too. So for group motivation and support, when I finally committed to the Withings platform, I went ALL in and got 6 trackers + the Withings scale as Christmas presents to myself and everyone around me. The fact that it works on both mobile platforms is a big plus. As was getting a group of us on this at the same time. Our friendly competition has definitely pushed me on the days I felt like slacking off.

3. Accurate enough. When I've gone on hikes and walks with friends who run, we've ended up with roughly the same number +/1 100 steps (albeit different calorie counts) at the end of the trail. So while it might not exactly match the listed distance on a trail you've gone in terms of miles, it is at least consistent enough with itself which is the most important thing. Also, while it might log a few steps as I'm moving the pulse from the strap to my pocket and vice versa, it consistently does that so I'm going to know on any given day if I've done net more or less.

4. Has motivated me. I wasn't sure how well this thing would work, but the simple act of having a concrete measure of my activity has motivated me to move and do more than any other system I'd set up for myself before. I periodically glance at my tracker during the day, and find myself adjusting (ok an extra-long route to the store, maybe stepping in place while I'm on the phone, pacing while I watch TV). Knowing exactly how much I've done means there's no excuse for me to "feel like I've done a lot". I know if I've been active. Or not.

5. Good customer service. I'd read online that people have had problems with their customer service. My personal experience was far from that. 5 days after I got the tracker, my clip holder broke. Personally I think it's poorly designed as the repeated act of taking the clip in and out of the holder every night to move put in your night armband for sleep tracking is going to add a lot of strain to the corner of the clip. Well I emailed customer service and they offered to replace my clip for free. I just sent them my proof of purchase and 9 days later a package arrived from France. I can't believe they sent the replacement from France but I'm happy to have the replacement.

6. Detailed app and web interface. I haven't seen the competitor apps, but for me, the web site and the app contain all the information I need. At a glance, I can see my overall trends (compared to the normal range), and I can see my weekly trends of when I'm sleeping, how well I'm sleeping, when I'm most active. I tried integrating MyFitnessPal. I couldn't stick with that kind of dedicating food logging, but if you're that kind of person, the integration gives you a complete in/out/impact picture.

7. Decent battery life. I'd say your tracker will last well over a week with regular use. And it charges back up quickly (maybe 15 minutes). The first days I got my tracker I was religiously syncing my tracker with my phone several times a day a few days later I'd only used about a bar of battery.

That said the device does have some limitations:

1. The plastic clip is really fragile. I've read reviews of people having problems with the clip falling out of the holder. To be safe, I keep the pulse in my pocket. At $99 (or $70 during the Christmas sale), I sure don't want to be dropping and losing this thing that often.

2. Some sort of data override would be nice. Given that the sleep tracker works by being strapped to your body, the assessment of light and deep sleep (or being awake) is measured by your amount of movement. I can be prone to insomnia, but sometimes that involves just lying awake and feeling frustrated. It usually doesn't involve thrashing around like a mad person because I'm so upset I'm awake. So the tracker has mistakenly taken my lack of motion to mean I'm in blissful deep sleep. I wish! It'd be nice in those cases to add manual entries (the way you can with weight) to add notes. But in generally there is a correlation where more deep sleep (or sleep overall) has resulted in feeling more rested the next day.

Bottom line: The results

How are the results? This was a gift to myself for Christmas. Since then, I've used the tracker every day and have committed to doing 10,000 steps every day. I didn't change my diet and still continued to eat a few pieces of chocolate and some kind of dessert once a day. This is not to say I prescribe this as the best way to get healthy. I just happen to have a healthy love of food and was also curious to see what straight up physical activity would do to my weight. I've never been overweight and lead a relatively active lifestyle, but 8 months of living off mayonnaise laden hotdogs while living in Chile did leave me a little plumper than I cared to stay

So 19 days into this I've walked an average of 73K steps every week and slept an average of close to 8 hours. I have gone from 111 lbs to a trendline average of 108 lb (naturally my weight will fluctuate at every measure but it steadily goes down.). I feel great and am feeling as motivated as I was on day one. Short of accidentally washing this thing or losing it, I'm going to keep using the Pulse and keep tracking! This device has been one of my favourite purchases in recent memory.
text_fidelity_b: Withings Pulse Wireless Activity Tracker + Sleep and Heart Rate Monitoring, Black

90 Degree By Reflex High Waist Fleece Lined Leggings with Side Pocket - Yoga Pants First of all, i bought this pants not entirely for yoga and thus i picked the one with pockets. I needed a pair of leggings with fleece that i can walk my dog during winter (in California!!). Don't judge me...but i am terrified of the cold. I bought the pants in two sizes, two colors; all with pockets.

FIT:
"M" and "S" fits me perfectly because the material is super stretchy and extremely comfortable. I'm 5'6 and 133lbs. "M" has the length that would wrap around the heel nicely and it doesn't feel bulky. I ended up taking the "S" simply because it was in black and i didn't want to take the trouble of returning. But on the hindsight, i would have preferred the "M" so i can pull it over my heel and not worry about wearing out the material over time.

COMFORT:
The fleece is very smooth and comfy. Definitely not a thin legging that you can wear underneath a pair of skinny jeans (unfortunately!). The pockets do add on the extra thickness.

WARMTH:
In an evening of ~50F, wearing just the leggings, socks and a pair of running shoes still left my feet feeling cold (again, don't judge the Californians..it's just me!). I couldn't walk my dog comfortably unless i start jogging to build up the heat. When I swapped my running shoes with a pair of Uggs/boots that gave me more coverage, it helped a lot. I've seen reviews where people would wear it outdoor in the snow under some snow pants... i dont know if I can make the same comparison.

Overall, i just love how comfortable the pants are. Not super expensive but also not as cheap.
text_fidelity_b: 90 Degree By Reflex High Waist Fleece Lined Leggings with Side Pocket - Yoga Pants

text_fidelity_a:
Pelican Self Inflating Sleeping Pad w/Pillow & Arm Rest, Camping Gear - Waterproof Foldable Lightweight Air Mattress - Memory Foam Sleeping Mat for Hiking, Backpacking - Travel Accessories - Black I use Pelican cases for work all the time, so I was intrigued at how they would handle camping gear like this. At first I was a little bit disappointed in the "self inflation" part. But once I understood what it means, I really do appreciate it now.
The only truly inflatable part are the side bars (which prevent you from rolling off the mat) and the pillow part. The middle is just memory foam with a familiar looking Pelican style valve on the bottom. If you've ever bought a memory foam mattress online, you know how this works- it comes in a vacuum sealed bag devoid of air, but once you cut it the air whooshes in and the mattress inflates to normal size. That's sort of what this "self inflation" is. You open the valve, the memory foam inside puffs itself up and becomes a more comfortable mat that is noticeably thicker than it was a moment ago. Seal the valve back up, and you can lie down on it and it honestly feels better than it looks!
Once you are done using it, allow the air to leave the side pockets and pillow, release the valve at the bottom, and roll it up. While rolling it, the air will leave the valve at the bottom, and when you've reached the end, just close the valve again to seal it from trying to open and inflate again. It's actually a pretty smart design once you understand it, I just didn't know what to expect before it arrived. I hope this review helps explain it to future buyers who might be expecting a larger self inflating mattress.
text_fidelity_b: Pelican Self Inflating Sleeping Pad w/Pillow & Arm Rest, Camping Gear - Waterproof Foldable Lightweight Air Mattress - Memory Foam Sleeping Mat for Hiking, Backpacking - Travel Accessories - Black

text_fidelity_a:
Osprey Stratos 50 Men's Backpacking Backpack There is a reason why Osprey's are one of the best selling packs on the market today. They combine great features, comfort, durability, and usefulness into one package. It has a 50L capacity.

First off, if you haven't had a new pack in a while, stop and get a new one. My old pack was one from the 90s, and though it served me well for many day hikes and overnighters, it was time to move up. And a step up it is.

First off the pack is light. New materials make this a very light pack. Also, the straps are highly adjustable for various sized people, so whether you are 5'6" or 6'2" you'll be able to find a comfortable fit for you. Another important thing is the fully padded shoulder and hip straps, which makes carrying heavy loads bearable and comfortable. The rig and internal frame is rigid, but not too heavy while not sacrificing comfort and adjust-ability.

Another aspect of this pack that is so great is how it carrys the load. Previous packs carried the load directly on your back, with much of the weight on the shoulders. This distributes the weight with more on your hips, saving your shoulders. It also keeps the pack a bit off your back. At first it feels a bit weird, as the center of gravity and weight distribution is a bit different that I was used to, but after a few miles I hardly felt I was carrying anything at all! Also, with the ventilated back, it keeps your back from rubbing against the pack and sweating so much.

There are pockets galore, including some nice zippered pouches on the hips, I use for my GPS, chapstick, etc. Mesh side pockets are good for medium sized water bottles, or whatever you want to put in there, snacks, flashlight, etc. Back pocket good sized as well.

The top flap is large and can hold a lot of stuff, and has a retainer for your keys. It can also be detached completely.

Top loading is a cinch, as it has multiple straps for tightening or loosening the pack to accommodate larger or smaller packouts. The large inside pocket can also be accessed by side zippers.

Inside the pack there is a pocket for your hydration system, that can feed up through the top of the pack and attaching to one of your shoulder straps.

The bottom of the pack features a tent/sleeping back compartment that can be accessed by the bottom zipper. And finally at the very bottom of the pack is a small compartment that contains a handy and very useful rainfly. No need to buy another! I still would waterproof the rainfly with repellent for extra rain proofing.

The only drawback I see is a lack of molle loops, so as a previous reviewer noted means it is not meant for heavy duty hikes. I still feel it would be nice to have a couple because I like to attach my flip flops and a few rags to the outside of the pack. Having one or two would be very useful.

Overall this is a really good packs for long day hikes or light overnights. 50L gives you plenty of capacity for light backpacking or a heavy duty day hike. Well worth the money, and with the quality of Osprey and their wonderful guarantee, who can go wrong with this?
text_fidelity_b: Osprey Stratos 50 Men's Backpacking Backpack

text_fidelity_a:
Concept2 Model D Indoor Rowing Machine (Gray) This review is coming from a dumpy middle-aged woman with a hip replacement who *thought* she was going to buy a treadmill. I started comparison shopping for treadmills even though spending $1000 or more on a machine instead of just going outside for a walk seemed kind of ridiculous, even in the snow. Then I ran across an article that mentioned rowing machines as the best overall piece of home exercise equipment. Some of my college dorm mates rowed on the women's 8 and it was like the light went on. The unanimous glowing reviews for the Concept2 Model D sold me on this machine and I ordered it direct from Concept2.

After about a month I can recommend rowing without reservation. The machine itself is built like a tank. It took about 20 minutes to put it together and about 2 minutes to figure out how to separate the parts for storage. It takes about 20 seconds to actually pull the machine apart and tuck it away in a corner when I'm not using it, which I do every day. Separated, it takes up the floor space of a medium-sized refrigerator. Together, it's about 9 feet long and a possible trip hazard. I use it on a carpeted floor and haven't noticed any problems with slipping and the machine doesn't need to be leveled. Gunk tends to accumulate on the rollers under the seat, which would probably go unnoticed if you don't pull the sled off and tip it up, but it's easy to clean.

I spent the first week focusing on correct technique and not killing myself. The machine comes with two booklets, a memory card, and a bottle of chain oil. The Indoor Rowing booklet has a lot of good information on proper form and suggested workouts starting from your very first day. There are also videos and active user forums on the Concept2 website. I've been following the suggestions, started slowly, set the damper at 3 and have left it there. Most nights I row from 25 to 40 minutes followed by stretching (recommended: AM/PM Stretch with Madeleine Lewis or AM Yoga for Your Week with Rodney Yee). I spent a lot of time on form and kept my stroke rate at about 18-19 spm. Slow, right? But I don't get sloppy and as I get stronger it seems that upping the stroke rate doesn't really improve my performance all that much. Before I started rowing, the morning routine was to get out of bed with cramping in my thigh and buttocks that nearly put me in tears. No joke: this disappeared overnight as soon as I started rowing. I felt a little soreness, mostly in my upper back, but zero lower back pain and no cramping AT ALL. One week of this was worth the $900.

The rowing machine puts you in total control of your workout in terms of how hard and how fast you want to work, and doesn't require you to do anything other than row harder or faster - there's no incline or speed buttons to push like with a treadmill. The rowing motion feels quite natural to me and time slides by. I actually look forward to my rowing time, and even though I'm still just getting started there is nothing about this that makes me feel like I won't be looking forward to my rowing time any less by next year. Plus, I expect by then I will be getting a lot more competitive about upping my pace. Update: Concept2 has a 100,000m between Thanksgiving and Christmas challenge. UPS delivered the Monday after Thanksgiving and without even trying I'm within 15K with 4 days to go. That's how cool rowing is.

If you're on the fence about which home exercise machine to buy, do yourself a favor and buy a rowing machine. Do yourself an additional favor and buy a Concept2.
text_fidelity_b: Concept2 Model D Indoor Rowing Machine (Gray)

text_fidelity_a:
GoSports Fitness Core Hub Plank Board with Smart Phone Integration for Full Body Workouts - Blue or Red So far so good with this GoSports Core Hub Fitness Plank Board with Smart Phone Integration. I’d seen a similar product in commercials and wondered if it would actually work for planking - or was it a gimmick. When I had the chance to grab this GoSports Core Hub Fitness Plank Board with Smart Phone Integration I took it, hoping it would add to my workout options. For various reasons I prefer not to plank directly on the ground, so would this be of help? The answer for me is, yes. As I continue to adjust to using it.

It arrives with the platform itself, pump, and instructions. One assembles the platform simply by pumping air into the ball on the bottom. My wife and I found this was a two person job - the long needle easily went in, however, it also easily pumped out until I had her hold it in place. At that point the ball quickly and easily pumped to full size. Pulling the needle out the air stayed in and there was no leaking - with nothing to plug it - and a week later holds the air perfectly. They included a second pin for the end of the pump - great if the first breaks or is lost, but we’ve found the first one wouldn’t even come off after we secured it.

There is a plastic covering on the phone “t” so don’t forget to remove it. It easily comes off and the foam under holds the phone in place just fine - though I haven’t used the phone or any app for working out at this point - I do have it there for stop watch.

I’ve put some pounds on since surgery so I wondered how it would hold the weight and so far it’s fine. I don’t feel any weakness or bowing or any issue in holding me up. As a shorter guy with shorter arm length I do find that positioning my arms in a spot to make placement comfortable is not exact. In fact, I end up testing my forearms a bit to hold on. And it’s taking time to find the best spot for being comfortable on the platform. Plus having the platform lay right in oder to balance correctly. Still working it, but also, still getting a solid workout. In fact I come away each time feeling the burn and it’s been a solid way to plank. It can be used in either the kneeling or full out, extended leg position and while I’ve only done it fully extended, I can see the benefits to both options.

So, does the movement and/or height add to the benefit of planking? I have to think it does. I like being up off the floor and having a nice, comfortable surface under my arms. As for the movement, it does work the fuller core area and I feel the burn in more than just one spot. I’ve only done this for a week, twice a day most days, and I’m doing better at time at the end of that week. I will maybe add in the app-games, but right now that is not my personal interest - but I can see how it could add to the fun (I’m not a gamer).

Any cons? So far it’s a little too early to know overall - will the board last, how does the app work...
I did notice there is a ’sound’ when laying on the board under the forearms. It seems like it might indicate the surface material could separate from the hard plastic base.

As long as the ball holds up - and I so far do not see why it won’t hold up - it can be a good, solid exercise platform. But that foam on the top needs to also remain. If that comes off, it will affect the platform itself. So far it’s fine, but again, what does that sound mean - other times I’ve heard it things have separated.

In the end I so far believe this GoSports Core Hub Fitness Plank Board with Smart Phone Integration is a great find and will help me with my workouts and to improve physically. text_fidelity_a:
Augason Farms Cheese Blend Powder Certified Gluten Free Long Term Food Storage Everyday Meal Prep Large Can, 1.48 kg I buy Augason products when they are on sale. Been doing this on and off for a few years now. Always been a bit of a "prepper", since I was a toddler it seems, haha (In my 40s now). I has served me well through power outages, sicknesses, unemployment, and even bigger stuff like the pandemic, and now... *vaguely gestures around* everything else that is going on. I've never been one to be without when anything has come up. I never did "emergency food" if only because I didnt have the budget. I would stick with typical foods and try to store them well. Well now I have a little more wiggle room in my budget, and with the on and off sales of long term storage (20+ years), I take advantage when I can. I remember buying some Augason eggs back in 2019 for $19. Today? $33-56 for same container, depending on the day.

And so, I haven't opened this 3lbs 4 ounce container of cheese blend powder.. sorry. I dont intend to any time soon. But I wanted to shore up my options. Having some soups and such just adds flavor to other options used. I can add more veg, or a protein, or beans, or simply have some bread to dip into it. Or I can use as way to flavor something. I have a slew of reviews to write on various Augason products, and so they will all be pretty much the same: Super long term storage (25+ years), no matter what the weight, it will be stuffed into a #10 can (that reads, "number ten", not ten pound. I see that mistake in reviews). They keep sizes uniform. Next size up is a round bucket, next size up gets into the rectangular buckets. This is for storage that can be uniform, etc. So yes, you may buy a 7 ounce item that is volume wise that takes up a smidge of space, but it will be packed into a large #10 container. Just remember, all food products are sold based on weight, not volume anyway. All of my containers have been in perfect condition. Maybe one day soon I will try one container out and see how the product actually is.

Everyone's SHTF scenario varies. It could be bad weather (tornadoes, hurricanes, blizzards, ice storms), could be illness, could be road trip gone wrong (you do keep supplies in your car too, right?!), could be unemployment, or power outage, or lack of transportation, or oven/fridge/other appliance break down, or bigger stuff like plagues, food shortages, supply chain issues, *cough WW3 cough*, etc. No matter the situation we all need some things to get by: we need is food, water, shelter, some hygeine and medical stuff, and so on. You dont have to stack "emergency supplies" but you do need to stack shelf stable food items. Buy a few extra things every single time you go to the store. If you get to a spot that you feel comfortable and have the budget, then grab the "emergency" items like Augason offers. I like adding it in and just forgetting about it.

I give 5 stars because the cans always are in perfect condition, they have regular sales, are good about shipping items as soon as they can, have lots of items to choose from, and so far seem to be of good quality.
text_fidelity_b: Augason Farms Cheese Blend Powder Certified Gluten Free Long Term Food Storage Everyday Meal Prep Large Can, 1.48 kg

text_fidelity_a:
FILA Accessories Home Gym Kit This gym arrives in a small box. It comes in 26 pieces with one tightening key and one written "exercise" sheet but no assembly instructions. I also needed to use a hammer (not included) when assembling the pull-up bar.

I am somewhat mechanically inclined, so I was able to use the visual pictures on the box (see last two pictures) to assemble the gym. The screws that attached the arms to the long bar of the pull-up bar caused me a lot of trouble. I eventually had to hammer the screws into the "square" hole when no amount of turning would screw them in. If it were not for that difficulty, I would have had this assembled in about 20 minutes instead of 45 minutes.

- The ab wheel is easy to use and rolls nicely on a carpeted floor.

- The push-up bars are a bit disappointing because the foam handles keep sliding back and forth when I try to do push-ups. The foam needs to be snug and not loose like it is. It requires certain positioning to keep these foam handles from moving.

- The pull-up bar is not something I will use as intended for two reasons. I feel like I will rip my molding off the door frame if I use this or mar my wall surface. Also, I am not (nor was I ever) strong enough to pull up my body weight. Nevertheless, this can be used on the floor as sort of a push-off bar as shown in the last picture.

Overall, I am disappointed in this set. The exercise sheet provided is not an exercise sheet at all. There are no assembly instructions, which is a requirement to me. I also do not like that the foam handles on the push up bars slide around and are unstable. If the foam handles stayed in place, I would have rated this four stars. However, because I consider that a defect coupled with the fact that not everyone will find it so easy to assemble without instructions, I am giving this three stars. Nevertheless, this is a low-budget option for those that do not mind the lack of instructions.

PHOTOS:
Photo one and two are the front and back of the only instructions provided, which is supposed to be an exercise sheet but has nothing to do with exercises. This sheet is a useless piece of paper to me. Photo three includes a picture of the two push up bars and the one ab wheel. Picture four includes the reverse (non-business) side of the pull-up bar and picture five is the business-side (the side where the user positions him or herself) of the bar. The last two pictures are the front and back of the box cover showing the product in use and is what helped me assemble this gym.
text_fidelity_b: FILA Accessories Home Gym Kit

text_fidelity_a:
W WSTOO Snorkel Mask with Latest Dry Top Breathing System,Fold 180 Degree Panoramic View Full Face Snorkel Mask Anti-Fog Anti-Leak with Camera Mount,Snorkeling Gear for Adults and Kids We are preparing for our trip to Costa Rica and wanted to try a full face snorkel and this one looked pretty good. And right out of the box and after just a couple strap changes I have to say that it is very comfortable on. I have been reading about them and I was a little concerned about CO2 build up and problems getting the mask off in an emergency but that does not seem to be any problem.

We did run a test of the mask in the city pool and it was surprisingly free of leaks. I did have problems with some leakage when I dove and it does seem to do better when simply cruising along the surface as the mask changes its fit when diving. Breathing turned out to be very comfortable and the flipping snorkel was great. We had some issues with fogging immediately (note it was in a car at 7 degree Fahrenheit and brought into a steamy indoor pool.) but that seemed to have cleared up well once the mask was warm.

Clarity was not the best. It was definitely ok for my purposes, but there is a little distortion, especially in the bend of the lense. It is still definitely workable but a little distorted. I would guess there is better glass out there, but this is a pretty low price point. It should meet our expectations for the trip, but probably will not exceed them.

-----

Reaction after the trip - There was a bit of struggling with leaks around the mask, especially along eyes and hairline. It did fog a little, and it was hard to dive without all of these things getting a little worse. But if I stayed on the surface and took the mask off occasionally to clear water and fog. It worked well enough. It was a little bulky to pack and if you are serious about your snorkeling (we did about 6 hours in six days.) you may want a better fitting mask.
text_fidelity_b: W WSTOO Snorkel Mask with Latest Dry Top Breathing System,Fold 180 Degree Panoramic View Full Face Snorkel Mask Anti-Fog Anti-Leak with Camera Mount,Snorkeling Gear for Adults and Kids

This cooler is incredibly well-made and I'm thrilled that I got it! (I ended up buying everyone their favorite team's cooler in this same brand, and they were a huge hit over the holidays!)

The first great surprise when it arrived was that it is made by Coleman, with tags on it to prove it. Coleman doesn't make bad stuff, in fact, they have a long history of well-made products, so that was a really nice bonus.

On top of that, there are all kinds of quality extras built into it. For example, when you lift the lid, there is a mesh ice-pack holder built right into the top of it. On the outside of it, there are mesh holders on each side (I use them for napkins, straws, or nutrition bars). Then in the front there is a nice zippered compartment that you can securely stash a few things in. The zippers are high quality and the materials, inside and out, are high quality as well. The strap is wide, strong and adjustable. Another nice perk is that it has a little pad where the strap will go over the shoulder, which really makes carrying it much more comfortable. The cooler holds a lot, and really does a great job at keeping things nice and cold. I just put my ice packs in it with our bottles, sandwiches, etc., and we are good to go.

I also got one of these coolers for a friend who is disabled and likes to keep a cooler next to her bed. Well, she'd gotten fed up with coolers that didn't keep things cold for very long and she had switched to using a spaghetti pot (for real!) with ice packs in it, to keep her ginger ale chilled, for constant nausea. She said that with a few frozen ice packs in it, she actually can go two whole days without having to replace the ice packs. She also said it fits great on her scooter when she's on the go.

Made by Coleman, like I said, and with lots of nice features, this high quality cooler is a must-have and a great gift. Check out the same cooler with other team logos. Just make sure you get the one like this one from "TLG8," to get the high quality one I just described. Thanks for reading my review. Hope it helped someone.

text_fidelity_a:
Caboodles Tote I selected this bag to replace my laptop bag, which was taken by my college-age son when his previous bag failed him. My personal preference in bags is actually a messenger style bag, not a tote, so I wasn’t sure if this would be my new go-to bag or if I needed to keep shopping. It has proven to be a good bag and I am mostly happy with it.

This bag is large enough to handle a 15” laptop, but it is better suited for a smaller-sized laptop or tablet. It isn’t going to handle anything bigger, the limiting dimension being the height, unless you’re content with not zipping the bag or having the contents obstruct the handles. Of course there is room to put others things in the bag with said laptop too, so it’s not just a laptop sleeve.

The bag itself is made of a tight nylon weave with vinyl handles, a vinyl divider and an outside vinyl pocket. It is not impervious to cuts and nicks but the nylon is fine enough that it should resist most hazards such as desk corners. I looked this bag over very carefully and found no cuts, nicks or blemishes in the materials, the stitching is straight and there are no loose threads. Overall, it is made well.

If I could change two things...I would have used canvas instead of nylon which holds up better to frequent use and tends to be stronger. Time will tell if this bag will withstand steady use, but so far it’s faring well enough and showing no signs of fatigue. Also, I would have reinforced the bottom with a heavier material which is the one place where this bag seems most likely to eventually fail.

My preference in bags is still a messenger bag; that said, this is a decent bag that seems to be made well and is large enough to handle my laptop. If you prefer a tote bag to either a messenger or backpack, this one is worth consideration.
text_fidelity_b: Caboodles Tote

text_fidelity_a:
SHELL Ride Foldable Electric Scooter for Adults, Max Speed 15-20 MPH, Max Range 17-20 Miles, Dual Braking Systems, Maintenance-Free (no Flat) Tires, Cruise Control & Ergonomic Grips [[VIDEOID:f93075686d622a2883750f40a78d44a4]] I'm all over the place with this, but here's what I've got - received a unit, wiring was exposed and I believe was shorting against the metal pole (you can see the wiring). I wrapped it with electrical tape. Wiring connector which you absolutely have to do before you put the screws in was rough. I did not think I was going to be able to plug it in without bending prongs. Wiring (low voltage): bad.

Instructions for locking and unlocking the handle need to include "put your shoulder into it" as it's not possible as far as I can tell to 1) steady the unit with your foot, 2) press forward with 15-20 pounds of force at the top while 3) pulling up on locking ring. I put a video up of how I have to do it. Maybe I'm special.

App, at least on my phone fails nonstop while connecting if it's still searching for other devices. Needs a little work. App is kind of useless.

Used battery appears to be a guess... I rode 8 miles on flat surfaces and blew through 50% of the battery on the first 2.5 miles and 30% on the next 5.5... I stress flat. I will record elevation changes next time. Maybe after a few runs it figures it out. I don't know. part of that was back and forth because I thought I was going to be stranded when it hit close to 50 at 2.5 miles. Basically I could not estimate how much I had left, and it turned out I had a lot of battery left when I finished and it said I had 30%.

Yes, I measured how many watt hours I put into the thing. Either it didn't fill up or I used roughly half a tank to propel myself 8 miles in performance mode at full tilt.

Top speed I can achieve according to the scooter is about 17mph. This is on flat surfaces, going down a slight hill. Breeze pushing me forward, etc. I'm about to take the thing to the gym and see if it can exceed 17mph with no weight on it on a treadmill, but it feels like that's the upper speed it claims.

I have not verified that's the real upper speed, will slap my phone and Google Maps in Driving mode on it later to find out.

Rattles... something in the back of it rattles and I can't locate it. It's not terrible, but man it's noticeable.

As for performance - I decided to test with 290 pounds on the unit. That's me, some weights/equipment, and 70 pounds over the limit. It'll handle that. It'll go up small hills and struggle. It was more powerful than expected. Not sure the battery life on that but that one got a few miles. Wouldn't advise that level.

Weld and most quality of this is good. App is meh and you really don't need it for anything. They could display all of this on the unit. At this price the lack of the ability to lock the unit from being turned on feels odd.

The brick of a charger that only puts out 90 watts seems excessive.

It's fun, rides well, app needs work, is expensive for how bad the internal wiring and app is, is mostly quality except that wiring is garbage.

Really, I'm all over the place with this. No judgement so far except on the app and wiring.
text_fidelity_b: SHELL Ride Foldable Electric Scooter for Adults, Max Speed 15-20 MPH, Max Range 17-20 Miles, Dual Braking Systems, Maintenance-Free (no Flat) Tires, Cruise Control & Ergonomic Grips

text_fidelity_a:
Light & Motion Vis 360 Plus Bike Helmet Light I commute by bike and I'm obsessed with seeing and being seen at night. I have a 650 lumen TerraLUX TT-5 flashlight (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B009WFA4KU/) strapped to my handlebars as my primary light. I added this helmet-mounted light set as redundancy / extra security. I've had it about a month now.

This is a pretty good light. It's fairly bright, and I like that it has amber LED's on both sides of both the front and rear light. This makes you visible from any angle (hence the "360" in the name). Having gotten used to the blinding, virtual daylight of the 650 lumen flashlight on my handlebars, the 250 lumens that this light puts out on max doesn't seem quite bright enough to me. But I could get home safely with this alone if my flashlight were to fail, so it's bright enough.

Things I like about helmet-mounted lights in general:
1) You can aim the light wherever you need it. It's handy for checking out turns before you've made the turn. And I can now see the display from my bike computer without having to wait for a streetlight! And when I'm off my bike, I can see my lock, into my trunk bag, etc.
2) They increase visibility and therefore safety.
3) You'll probably leave them mounted to your helmet most of the time, so you're less likely to forget them. And if you're locking your bike up somewhere you'll probably take your helmet with you, so you'll automatically take your lights too - less chance of theft.

Things I like about this light in particular:
1) It's one of the brighter ones available.
2) It actively aims LED's in every direction, making you highly visible.
3) It's rechargeable and charges via USB.

Things I don't like about helmet-mounted lights in general:
1) They add weight to your head / neck.
2) They can get knocked around. I take my bike on the train for a portion of my commute, and when we near my stop I have my helmet on and am ready to get my bike out of the rack to disembark; meanwhile other riders are trying to get to their bikes. I frequently bang one or the other of the lights on the overhand above the bikes while we're all jostling around. Also, when I take my helmet off I feel I have to be more careful about stowing it so the lights don't get knocked about.

Things I don't like about this light in particular:
1) It's surprisingly heavy, and it's unbalanced. The front light is virtually weightless. The rear light, which has the battery pack, is surprisingly heavy. I invested in a very nice, "barely there" helmet that weighs virtually nothing. This light makes it feel like a brick. Obviously it's not that heavy, but it is heavier than I expected. And I don't like that all the weight is to the rear. This is okay when I'm leaning forward in riding position, but when I'm stopped at a light or otherwise upright, the weight is pulling my head back.
2) I find the rubberized button to turn it on / change modes difficult to feel and manipulate while I'm riding. If I don't take the train home, my commute is an hour and 15 minutes. To save battery I have it on low when I'm riding on well-lit streets and switch to high otherwise. I've had this light almost a month and I'm not getting better at feeling / adjusting the light. It takes concentration away from riding while I fiddle with it.
3) The tail light mode is not adjustable. It does this odd, slow fade-in / fade-out and that's it. You can't make it be always on, and you can't make it actually flash.
4) You can't have just the taillight on. Once the headlight's on, you can turn the taillight off independently, but you can't ride with just the taillight.
5) The battery is not replaceable. My flashlight / headlight runs on a replaceable, rechargeable battery, which means I can keep a spare battery in my pouch and be sure I have enough battery to get home. I can also ride with one battery while the other's at home recharging. With this light, if the battery runs out you can't use the light until you get to a USB charger. And it takes a good few hours to recharge, so you can't go riding for the hours it takes to recharge. And the low battery indicator is tucked away at the bottom of the taillight, and is only visible after you've plugged it in to recharge, so that doesn't help. So you'd better keep it charged.
6) You can change the angle of the front light, but only in discrete clicks. Each click is a very small angle of change on the device, but changes where the light hits the road by about 20'. I frequently want the light right in between two of the clicks and I can't put it there.
7) The helmet mounts strike me as odd. The front light slides into it's mount and clicks in place, but it slides in from the bottom. That means the if the clicky thing ever fails the light will slide out. If it slid in from the top gravity would keep it in place. And the rear light presses on with four tabs clicking into four slots. You really have to pull on it to dismount it. Odd.

Hmmm. Looking at this review there are way more things in the "don't like about this light" section than elsewhere, which makes it seem like I don't like this light. That's not true. None of the "don't likes" are show-stoppers. I'm keeping the light and I do like it. They're mostly just areas where I feel like the light could be somewhat better. If you buy this light you'll definitely be seen, you'll see where you're going, and you'll probably be happy you have it. These are just my observations for whatever they may be worth to you.
text_fidelity_b: Light & Motion Vis 360 Plus Bike Helmet Light
